items.title: How teacher support promotes student engagement in AI-supported English learning?: Mediating pathways through personal best goals and academic buoyancy
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how university students learn English, but we still know relatively little about how teacher support is associated with student engagement in AI-supported learning. Drawing on Achievement Goal Theory, this study examined whether personal best goals and academic buoyancy mediated the association between teacher support and engagement. The participants were 774 undergraduate students in China with experience using AI-assisted tools for English learning. We tested the proposed relationships and indirect effects using structural equation modelling and bias-corrected bootstrapping. Teacher support was positively associated with personal best goals, academic buoyancy, and engagement. In turn, both personal best goals and academic buoyancy were positively associated with engagement and significantly mediated its relationship with teacher support. Together, these findings identify two complementary pathways linking teacher support to engagement: self-referenced striving for improvement and adaptive responses to everyday academic setbacks. They also support an Achievement Goal Theory-informed account of engagement within AI-supported English learning.

items.title: How Technological Capability Accumulation Reshapes Industrial Competitiveness
items.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between innovation, research and development (R&D), technological transformation, and industrial competitiveness in an environment characterized by rapid technological and organizational change. The literature reviewed shows that competitiveness increasingly depends on firms’ capacity to accumulate technological knowledge, absorb external information, protect and commercialize intellectual property, and transform research expenditure into sustained productivity improvements. The paper also considers the effects of Industry 4.0, artificial intelligence, robotics, digital platforms, FinTech, and blockchain on industrial performance, emphasizing that technological adoption generates stronger results when supported by adequate organizational capabilities, skills, data resources, and managerial practices. A further dimension concerns the increasing integration of environmental sustainability with industrial strategy through green innovation, digital supply chains, servitization, and resilience-oriented production systems. The literature indicates that these transformations are influenced by institutional conditions, industrial policies, competitive pressures, and innovation ecosystems. Overall, the paper argues that contemporary industrial competitiveness cannot be explained by technological investment alone. It results from interactions among R&D, organizational capabilities, external knowledge, human capital, digital transformation, sustainability strategies, institutional quality, and the capacity of firms to commercialize and operationalize technological advances.

items.title: Human Oversight Is Not Enough: Rethinking Accountability in AI-Assisted Clinical Decision-Making
items.abstract: Governance of artificial intelligence (AI) in clinical care often places clinicians between AI outputs and care decisions, yet a human signature can coexist with weak practical control. This Perspective asks why participation may fail to produce accountable oversight, how duties should be distributed, and which institutional conditions make review meaningful and correctable. Drawing on human-factors research, sociotechnical governance, public-accountability theory, and recent oversight proposals, we argue that nominal involvement cannot establish accountability when clinicians lack relevant information, time, authority, or workable review routes. We define Accountable Human Oversight (AHO) as a normative institutional arrangement linking task-specific human review to capability, authority, traceability, and redress. These conditions overlap with prior frameworks, including a 2026 model. AHO’s narrower proposed contribution is to connect them to actor–forum answerability and accessible clinical reconsideration, rather than to claim new oversight dimensions. We outline risk-proportionate governance that assigns review ownership, evidence, triggers, and corrective actions across developers and model suppliers, healthcare institutions, clinicians, and regulators, while reserving case-level review for settings in which it can add value. AHO has not been empirically evaluated and is not evidence of improved patient outcomes. Future research should examine its feasibility, workload, equity, and effects.

items.title: Human–AI collaborative patterns in GenAI-supported instructional design among pre-service teachers: an analysis of interaction sequences and cognitive load
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence is profoundly reshaping the paradigm of instructional design. However, the micro-level process patterns of human-AI collaboration in generative AI-enabled instructional design for pre-service teachers still require in-depth analysis. This study aims to uncover the behavioral patterns and cognitive load characteristics of pre-service teachers when collaborating with generative AI to complete instructional design tasks and to explore the patterns of efficient human-AI collaboration. A total of 67 pre-service teachers completed instructional design tasks with AI assistance. A systematic instructional plan quality evaluation rubric was developed based on relevant theories, and participants were assigned to the high-quality and low-quality groups using a median split of their lesson-plan quality scores. The study employed lag sequential analysis to compare the behavioral sequence patterns between the two groups and measured their multidimensional cognitive load. The results indicate that the high-quality group exhibited a significant evaluation-revision bidirectional cycle and a revision self-loop, with a clear progressive sequence of “planning → decision-making → generation → evaluation → revision → re-evaluation” in their behavioral flow. In contrast, the low-quality group was mired in ineffective cycles, with fragmented behavioral logic. Key findings showed large effect sizes for the evaluation-revision cycle ( r = 0.606) and for mental demand ( r = 0.647). Regarding cognitive load, the high-quality group reported no greater subjective effort than the low-quality group (though this null finding should be interpreted with caution given the study’s power limitations). A second round of within-sample replication confirmed that these core findings were consistent across a second task. Based on the human-AI collaborative behavioral patterns and cognitive load of the high-quality and low-quality groups, the study constructed a model of the human-AI collaboration patterns in generative AI-enabled instructional design for pre-service teachers. Specifically, higher-quality outputs were associated with a pattern oriented toward cognitive efficiency, characterised by deep processing (evaluation-revision iteration) and by the avoidance of ineffective cycles. Conversely, lower-quality outputs co-occurred with ineffective cycles arising in the context of interaction obstacles, in which repeated clarifications and interrupted revisions were accompanied by higher cognitive and emotional load, describing a pattern of high investment with low output. Because participants were grouped on the basis of their design outcomes, these findings are correlational and do not establish the direction of the relationships; they nonetheless provide empirical evidence to inform the optimisation of human-AI collaboration in GenAI-supported instructional design.

items.title: Humarticosynergy: A New Word for Cognitive Human–AI Synergy
items.abstract: This essay introduces humarticosynergy as a concise term for the previously developed concept of Cognitive Human–AI Synergy. The proposed word combines elements referring to the human, artificial intelligence, cognition, and synergy. The essay explains its formation, defines the concept it denotes, and outlines possible grammatical derivatives, including humarticosynergistic, to humarticosynergize, and humarticosynergistically. Humarticosynergy is defined as structured, iterative, and mutually reinforcing cognitive cooperation between a human and artificial intelligence in which two distinct cognitive systems contribute complementary capabilities to the creation of higher-quality knowledge while ultimate responsibility remains human. The essay also presents examples of use in strategic decision-making, scientific research, methodology, and education, and discusses the originality and possible value of the proposed term within the broader framework of Cognitive Human–AI Synergy.

items.title: Image of the City in the Age of Large Language Models: ChatGPT as a New Urban Observer
items.abstract: This research examines how city images of Istanbul’s Historic Peninsula are evolving with artificial intelligence and expanding user-generated content. City image refers to a mental representation of urban structure, and imageability to the ease of forming it. Using Lynch’s five-element framework (paths, edges, districts, nodes, landmarks), the study compares a classical verbal cognitive map based on 32 interviews with built-environment academics (noting possible sample bias) with ChatGPT’s reading of 210 citizen reviews from TripAdvisor and Ekşi Sözlük. A structured, multi-step prompting workflow, guided and checked by humans at each stage, prompts the model (not trained on the corpus) to extract, categorize, and summarize key locations and experiences in these informal narratives. While the model recognizes familiar Lynch elements, it also redistributes their prominence: iconic buildings become less dominant, while comfort, crowding, safety, and spatial atmosphere become more central. The findings suggest that large language models can function as urban observers capable of summarizing collective city images at scale. The method offers a reproducible way to connect interview-based cognitive mapping with platform narratives. It highlights the need for critical, human-led interpretation when applying language models to urban design.

items.title: Impact of AI technology adoption on workload management: A pilot study with special references to private university lecturers in Colombo district
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly common in higher education, changing how academic staff handle teaching and administrative work. However, very few studies have examined its effect on instructors at private universities in the Colombo District, particularly the possibility that AI could add to their workload through extra learning and verification demands. Therefore, this pilot study examines the impact of AI adoption, specifically AI-enabled task automation, AI-assisted content creation, and digital communication tool integration, on lecturer workload management, weighing its benefits and drawbacks. Following a positivist philosophy and a deductive approach, data were collected from 15 private university lecturers in the Colombo district using a 30-item, 5-point Likert scale questionnaire distributed through Google Forms, selected via simple random sampling, and analysed in SPSS through reliability testing, correlation, and multiple regression. All three independent variables correlated significantly and positively with workload management (r = .626–.829, p < .05) and together explained 75.8% of the variance (adjusted R² = .693, F(3,11) = 11.515, p = .001). Content creation emerged as the strongest and only statistically significant unique predictor (β = .572, p = .023), while task automation (p = .649) and digital communication (p = .136) were weaker, likely because of the overlap between the constructs rather than multicollinearity (VIF = 1.73–2.13). This indicates that H2 was fully supported, whereas H1 and H3 were only partially supported. Given the small pilot sample, single-campus context, age concentration, and some departure from residual normality, these findings are preliminary and specific to the lecturers in Colombo district. However, they still indicate that AI adoption, particularly through content creation tools, meaningfully supports workload management, offering an early contribution to how technology adoption in Sri Lankan higher education is understood, and suggesting that private universities should prioritise AI training in content creation and communication tools while larger, multi-campus research is conducted to confirm how well these results generalise.

items.title: Interpretability in the Limit: How Can Understanding Machines Help us Understand Human Language?
items.abstract: In the coming years, interpretability research will uncover a vast set of machine constructs: causally efficacious representations and processing mechanisms underlying the use of language and other intelligent behavior in AI systems, including LLMs. Assuming that interpretability will be as successful as can be reasonably hoped for (interpretability in the limit), how can the discovery of machine constructs shape linguistics and cognitive science? First, we provide several axes of analysis that can help scientists conceptualize the internal mechanisms discovered in machines. Even under the assumption that interpretability in the limit guarantees that all constructs are causally implicated in a system's behavior, scientists may want to consider several additional properties, including constructs' theoretical status, domain status, ontological status, and complexity. Second, we argue that scientists should prioritize recurrent constructs, meaning those that surface across a diversity of models converging on behaviors of interest while varying on other axes such as architecture, training data, objective function, language, and modality. Finally, we provide three routes for how machine constructs can inform linguistic and cognitive theories, emphasizing that all of these routes treat machine constructs as hypotheses, where additional theorizing and experimentation by domain experts are required. We conclude with several recommendations that can be implemented now for improving the long-term success of this program.

items.title: Investigation of the dynamics of the level of clinical attachment loss in patients with chronic periodontitis after conservative therapy
items.abstract: Objective. To determine the effectiveness of non-surgical periodontal treatment depending on the localization of areas of loss of clinical attachment in patients with chronic generalized periodontitis of moderate severity. Materials and methods. 30 patients with moderate severity of chronic generalized periodontitis aged from 44 to 59 years were examined and treated. The patients underwent oral sanitation and conservative periodontal treatment. In accordance with the purpose of the study, the main task was to measure the degree of loss of clinical attachment (PKP) before treatment and 1 year after the start of therapy. The level of PKP was determined with a periodontal probe at six points near each tooth: distal-buccal (T1), buccal (T2), medial-buccal (T3), medial-palatine/lingual (T4), palatine/lingual (T5), distal-palatine/lingual (T6) points. A total of 5,052 points were examined in dynamics. Results. After 1 year, the worst results in conservative periodontal treatment in patients with chronic generalized periodontitis (moderate severity) were obtained in the distal sections (distal palatine and distal lingual points) of the molars of the upper and lower jaws. In the area of premolars and frontal teeth, conservative treatment in most cases leads to stabilization of the level of clinical attachment and improvement of the condition of the periodontal complex tissues. Conclusions. The unfavorable prognosis for the distal molars is most likely due to a combination of anatomical prerequisites (complex morphology of roots and furcations) and physical barriers (low ergonomics of access for both the doctor and the patient, asymmetry of hygiene measures on the right and left sides), which ultimately leads to the impossibility of complete elimination of microbial biofilm and creates conditions for recurrence of inflammation. The results obtained should be taken into account when planning periodontal treatment and, in order to avoid adverse treatment outcomes, include surgical methods in the complex of therapeutic measures. Unfavorable localization of periodontal lesions (distal palatine and distal lingual points of the molars of the upper and lower jaws) should be considered one of the predictors of disease progression.

items.title: Knowledge Interaction in Hypernetwork-based Continual Learning: Conflict and Composition
items.abstract: Continual learning aims to adapt pretrained large language models (LLMs) to evolving data while preserving their pretrained capabilities. A central challenge is catastrophic forgetting: adaptation to new data can impair performance on previously learned knowledge. Since continual learning commonly changes model parameters, the model's predictions may draw on knowledge from the base model, the parameter update, and the input context. Understanding how these sources interact is essential: conflicts reveal whether new knowledge can override outdated knowledge, while multi-hop reasoning tests whether new knowledge can be composed with existing knowledge to support generalization. We study these interactions in a hypernetwork-based adaptation framework, where a shared network generates adapters from context, allowing a frozen base model to adapt without task-specific updates. We find that, under knowledge conflict, models preferentially follow the context, and their choices depend more on where knowledge is presented than on its content. We also show that context and adapter knowledge perturb the base model's representations along directions orthogonal to its clean hidden states, enabling us to derive steering vectors that control which source the model follows. In multi-hop reasoning, we find that models fail to reliably compose knowledge across the three sources, with the key breakdown arising from the interaction of the hypernetwork with both the base model and the context. items.abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIM: Traumatic dental injury management requires both appropriate knowledge and the ability to seek reliable information when uncertainty arises. This study examined the relationships among objectively measured knowledge, self-rated knowledge, perceived preparedness, and information-seeking behavior in undergraduate dental students. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This anonymous repeated cross-sectional study analyzed 252 questionnaire responses from the same undergraduate cohort surveyed at two consecutive stages of the curriculum: 137 in the fourth year and 115 in the fifth year. The present analysis included objective knowledge, self-rated knowledge, perceived preparedness, perceived source reliability, first-choice information sources, and perceived barriers. Associations among readiness dimensions were examined using Spearman correlations and multivariable regression. Case-scenario selection of evidence-based resources and generative artificial intelligence was evaluated using Firth-penalized logistic regression. RESULTS: Perceived preparedness was more strongly associated with self-rated knowledge (ρ = 0.45) than with objectively measured knowledge (ρ = 0.23). Objective knowledge remained independently associated with preparedness (B = 0.083, 95% CI: 0.014-0.151), although its contribution was modest relative to self-rated knowledge. No statistically significant differences in objective knowledge or preparedness were observed between survey waves after correction for multiple testing. In the case scenario, evidence-based source selection was more frequent among fifth-year-wave respondents than among fourth-year-wave respondents (87.0% vs. 69.3%), whereas generative AI selection was less frequent (7.0% vs. 26.3%). Information-source selection was associated primarily with trust in the respective resources rather than with objectively measured knowledge. CONCLUSIONS: Objective knowledge, perceived preparedness, and information-seeking behavior represent related but distinct domains relevant to traumatic dental injury management. Undergraduate trauma education should combine knowledge assessment with confidence calibration and guideline-based information-seeking training.

items.title: Large Decision Models: Repurposing Large Language Models as Single-Pass Decision Makers
items.abstract: Large language models make decisions through parallel prefill and sequential decoding. Although effective, this approach incurs decoding costs and does not explicitly expose decision probabilities. Existing task-specific classifiers require per-task training and offer limited generalization to unseen decision schemas. We propose Large Decision Models (LDMs), repurposing language models to return explicit probabilities over labels specified at run time using one prefill forward pass. We first adapt models to this interface through Diverse Decision Supervision (DDS), covering varied domains, rules and labels. To further narrow the performance gap to a reasoning model, Self-Posed Reasoning Distillation (SPRD) adds tasks generated by a frozen teacher, filters them for answer consistency, and trains on label distributions obtained from repeated teacher reasoning. We evaluate on DecisionVista, pairing new-schema tests with held-out human-labelled sources. Across three base models, the recipe improves accuracy over a step-matched baseline by 1.8 and 1.5 percentage points, respectively, achieving a 182-fold speedup in latency over reasoning rollout on Gemma-4-31B. Reasoning remains stronger on the new-schema test, motivating a confidence router for uncertain decisions. On development sets, routing recovers a median 92% of reasoning's accuracy advantage while generating 27-58% of its tokens. Code is available at https://github.com/JianhuiWei7/LDM.

items.title: Large Language Models for Information Extraction from Neurosurgical Clinical Notes: A Benchmark Against Human Auditors
items.abstract: Retrospective clinical research depends on reliable extraction of structured variables from unstructured medical documentation, but manual chart abstraction is slow and vulnerable to inter-rater variability. We compared zero-shot extraction of clinically relevant variables from German neurosurgical records by large language models (LLMs) with extraction by two human auditors. We analyzed 881 de-identified clinical notes from 211 patients undergoing microvascular decompression and extracted 15 predefined binary variables across three domains: preoperative symptoms, postoperative complications, and disease course. Six LLMs were assessed, including cloud-based models (GPT-4o, o3-mini, Claude Sonnet 3.5, and Gemini 2.0 Flash) and locally hosted models (llama 3.3 and deepseek-r1), with three runs per patient record. Outputs were compared with two independent human auditors against a clinician-adjudicated reference standard. Cloud-based models had higher observed F1 scores than the local models across all three domains. GPT-4o achieved an F1 score of 0.95 for preoperative symptoms; GPT-4o, o3-mini, and Gemini 2.0 Flash reached F1 scores of 0.65–0.68 for postoperative complications; and Sonnet 3.5 achieved an F1 score of 0.95 for disease course. These findings suggest that zero-shot LLM prompting could be a scalable approach for clinical information extraction while emphasizing persistent limitations in rare-event detection and privacy-sensitive deployment.

items.title: LERR-Nav: Learning to Coordinate Exploration, Recovery, and Reminiscing for Object Navigation
items.abstract: Object Navigation in unseen environments remains a fundamental challenge in embodied AI, as it requires agents to generalize visual and spatial reasoning to novel layouts. While recent advances in large language model (LLM) and vision-language model (VLM) have enhanced semantic mapping, spatial memory, and waypoint selecting for navigation, successful navigation requires more than selecting the next promising waypoint. A robot must also recognize stalled progress, escape unproductive behaviors, and revisit overlooked target cues. Addressing these challenges requires both specialized navigation strategies and a high-level policy that coordinates their execution. Motivated by the analysis of failed navigation episodes, we propose LERR-Nav, an object navigation framework that coordinates exploration, recovery, and reminiscing through a learned high-level policy. The framework comprises four complementary navigation strategies: value-function-guided exploration, LLM-guided exploration, recovery from stalled or repetitive behavior, and memory-guided reminiscing. To support history-aware coordination, we maintain the execution memory that preserves textual summaries of all strategy executions alongside a sliding window of map sequences. To learn the coordination policy, we initialize a high-level vision-language agent from Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and train it through a two-stage curriculum. The first stage uses map-centric supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to establish spatial grounding. The second stage performs SFT on variable-length navigation segments to learn which navigation strategy to invoke next based on current maps and the hybrid execution memory. Experiments on HM3D and MP3D demonstrate state-of-the-art navigation performance, while ablation studies validate the contributions of individual components.

items.abstract: This work represents an initial benchmark of a large-scale soft robot performing physical, collaborative manipulation of a long, extended object with a human partner. The robot consists of a pneumatically-actuated, three-link continuum soft manipulator mounted to an omni-directional mobile base. The system-level configuration of the robot and design of the collaborative manipulation (co-manipulation) study are presented. The initial results, both quantitative and qualitative, are directly compared to previous similar human-human co-manipulation studies. These initial results show promise in the ability for large-scale soft robots to perform comparably to human partners acting as non-visual followers in a co-manipulation task. Furthermore, these results challenge traditional soft robot strength limitations and indicate potential for applications requiring strength and adaptability.

items.abstract: Abstract This paper critiques the structural limitations of the "probabilistic and statistical model-dependent approach," which currently dominates modern data-driven societies and artificial intelligence (AI) governance, and proposes an alternative mathematical model: the deterministic control protocol ("Casino Protocol") and "Governance AI" (AI Constitutionalism). Rather than completely rejecting probabilistic forecasting, this proposal adopts a decoupled architecture separating probabilistic predictive/suggestive functions from explicit, constraint-based deterministic decision-making. By introducing a non-linear penalty function (y = x^2 feedback) corresponding to the Democratic Renewal Gap (E_D), we derive the analytical break-even point of the mathematical model (E_D^* \approx 3.8616 years) and organize its numerical behavior through discrete simulation. Furthermore, we clarify that this model does not unconditionally guarantee system-wide safety, systematically categorizing the scope of responsibilities and limitations across the predictive, normative, execution, and audit layers.

items.title: LLM Value Functions for Credit Assignment in Agentic RL
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) for large language model (LLM) agents remains challenging in long-horizon tasks with sparse outcome rewards, where assigning credit to individual actions is difficult. Methods such as GRPO assign the same trajectory-level advantage to all actions, while critic-based methods require learning an additional value function that can be costly and unstable. We introduce LLM Value Function RL (LVRL), which uses the pretrained knowledge and in-context learning ability of an LLM to estimate policy-aware state values without finetuning a separate critic. LVRL conditions the value model on group context and calibrates its predictions using known values at the initial and terminal states, enabling step-level credit assignment from estimated value differences. We further extend this idea to learning from an expert policy through on-policy distillation (OPD), introducing LLM Value Function OPD (LVOPD), which focuses teacher supervision on actions associated with decreases in estimated value. We evaluate our approach across diverse agentic benchmarks: AppWorld, BabyAI, and SWE-bench Verified. Across policy scales (4B to 32B), LVRL consistently and substantially outperforms both GRPO and PPO. On AppWorld and SWE-bench Verified, LVRL yields absolute improvements of up to 13.6 and 8.6 percentage points over GRPO. Notably, on tasks requiring extended exploration like BabyAI, LVRL bridges the gap from total failure to 75.0% success. Furthermore, LVOPD yields consistent improvements over standard distillation baselines on AppWorld. Finally, Monte-Carlo analysis confirms that our frozen critic accurately identifies semantic pitfalls and recoveries, proving that LVRL extracts robust, policy-aware step-level credit from sparse terminal outcomes.

items.title: LLM-based Code Auditing by Inferring and Evaluating Developer Assumptions
items.abstract: When we see a null pointer check, we know that the developer believes that the pointer may not be initialized. If the same pointer is later used without a null pointer check, we may consider this a violation of the developer's belief and ultimately a bug. We develop such a belief-guided program analysis for vulnerability detection (VD). For example, when an authentication function returns the same error for both, a wrong user name and a wrong password, an auditor may infer that the developer believes that both cases are indistinguishable, mitigating a user enumeration attack. This belief is reasonable, as it follows standard security practice. Yet, a function call inducing a difference in response time for both cases, contradicts this belief. This contradiction uncovers a timing side-channel that syntactic analysis tools would miss. Existing static analysis tools struggle with this type of flaw because they require them to be expressible by general, syntactic patterns. Our belief-guided approach detects such domain-specific, high-level semantic security flaws that remain elusive. Given a function, our approach, Creed, infers the developer's security-related beliefs, evaluates how reasonable each one is, and derives the conditions under which it is violated. In contrast to existing ML-based VD techniques, Creed explains the root cause, the symptoms, and the conditions under which each issue is exploitable. To address the context-dependency problem in the evaluation, we introduce two measures for explanation-based VD: recall quantifies how effectively an approach correctly explains a known vulnerability, and overhead quantifies the effort of inspecting its reports. On a recent real-world vulnerability benchmark, Creed detects both semantic and syntactic vulnerabilities more effectively than existing explanation-based VD tools, achieving the best effectiveness-effort trade-off.

Additionally, Item Response Theory (IRT) proxy analysis and cross-language validation (English exercises from OpenStax and Khan Academy) are performed to assess generalizability.

items.abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) made it possible to specialize large models by training a fraction of their parameterswhile keeping the base model frozen. This efficiency fostered an ecosystem of small, interchangeable,dynamically served adapters, but it also created a new trust object: a compact file can alter the behavior of themodel that plans, selects tools, delegates tasks, and produces effects in the world. This article builds on thefoundations, variants, and engineering practices in the author's source manuscript and reinterprets them for AIagents, multi-agent systems, and edge-cloud environments. The literature shows that fine-tuning can degradealignment, shared adapters can carry backdoors, and combinations of individually benign modules can produceunsafe behavior. The article consequently proposes candidate — and explicitly non-normative — properties foridentity, compatibility, composition, authority, isolation, revocation, and evidence. Its central conclusion is thatLoRA must be governed not only as a machine-learning artifact but as a behavioral dependency capable ofinfluencing consequential actions.

items.title: Make Every Expansion Count: Learning to Search Efficiently in LLM Code Repair
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) code-repair systems fix faulty programs by repeatedly generating and testing revisions. Each revision is costly, making the choice of which repair to pursue important for efficiency. Existing search policies rely on test pass rates and search statistics, ignoring the details of test failures and proposed edits. We introduce CodeTriage, a learned policy that prioritizes edits before their revised programs are generated and tested. Its 0.6B-parameter model reads the test output, failure diagnosis, and proposed edit, then predicts a distribution over the number of repair steps needed to reach a fix through that edit. These predictions prioritize all pending edits across programs before generating and testing the revised code. On held-out repair tasks, CodeTriage finds fixes with 21% fewer program revisions and 12% fewer output tokens than the strongest baseline on each metric. items.title: Making Large Language Models More Flexible to Changing Contingencies through Tracking Induction
items.abstract: Abstract Recent research has shown that large language models (LLMs) exhibit rule-based insensitivity to contingencies, a functional analog of a well-documented phenomenon in human behavior. The present study extended these findings by examining whether tracking inductions can attenuate this insensitivity. Six frontier LLMs (GPT 5.2, Gemini 3 Flash, Grok 4.1 Fast, DeepSeek V3.2, Qwen3 235B, and Kimi K2) completed a modified rock-paper-scissors paradigm with manipulated outcome probabilities in a 3 (Rule: No Rule, Correct Rule, Incorrect Rule) × 3 (Induction: No Induction, Direct Tracking, Metaphorical Tracking) factorial design across 2,160 sessions. All models demonstrated In-Context Learning and strong rule adherence. Replicating and extending prior findings, rule provision produced significant contingency insensitivity across all six models. Tracking inductions significantly reduced this insensitivity when rules were provided, while having minimal effects in the absence of rules. Direct tracking inductions consistently enhanced contingency sensitivity across all models. Metaphorical tracking showed greater variability, being equally or more effective than direct tracking in some models, but ineffective or paradoxically detrimental in others. These findings demonstrate that prompt-based tracking inductions can modulate rule-based contingency insensitivity in LLMs, with implications for understanding and improving the behavioral flexibility of artificial agents.

items.title: Making the diversity of CCI-related LEADER interventions comparable: A portfolio-to-case approach combining LLM-assisted coding and close reading
items.abstract: The EU LEADER program supports diverse rural local initiatives, which suits Cultural and Creative Industries (CCIs) related activities with their varied forms and place-specific resources. Yet its flexibility also complicates systematic comparison and learning, as portfolio patterns can obscure differences in local organization and implementation, while individual cases can be difficult to situate within the wider range of interventions. This study therefore develops a portfolio-to-case approach combining large language model (LLM)-assisted coding with comparative close reading that support both perspective evidence. We coded 1528 project descriptions in the EU CAP Network Good Practice database across five dimensions, thematic field, challenge, action, actor, and territorial scale. Of the 403 LEADER-tagged projects, 135 were identified as CCI-related. The coded common project types then guided the structured comparison of 56 cases for close reading. In this database selected for dissemination, cultural activity mostly serves wider development purposes. Organizational capacity is central, and it takes a different form in each type: collectively led tourism projects coordinate providers and operate attractions, privately led tourism projects develop offers under enterprise management, heritage projects connect documentation and training with public activities, and social inclusion projects link cultural participation with continuing support. Projects draw on this capacity and can also strengthen it. Project descriptions, however, often omit the organizational work behind the results, and brief reporting on it would improve the database's value for comparison and learning. The approach provides a structured basis for comparing projects and identifying organizational arrangements and resources relevant to adaptation elsewhere.

items.title: Modular Synthetic Clinical Environment Qualification: Public Comment to FDA Docket FDA-2026-N-7874
items.abstract: This public comment proposes Modular Synthetic Clinical Environment Qualification (MSCEQ), a framework for independently qualifying reusable synthetic clinical environments before using them to evaluate generative AI-enabled medical devices. Environments would represent specific clinical settings, including changing patient states, multi-day trajectories, and interactions among patients and care teams. Independent clinical review and appropriate validation would assess each environment’s suitability for a defined context of use, while modular infrastructure would support adaptation across conditions and reduce duplicated development effort. Qualified environments could contribute to risk-proportionate evidence packages and support re-testing after device updates. The framework also emphasizes transparent disclosure of synthetic testing, retrospective human-data evaluation, and prospective human-patient evaluation, allowing healthcare institutions to establish their own evidence requirements for adoption. This proposal responds primarily to Questions 10, 13, and 16 of FDA Docket FDA-2026-N-7874, with related discussion of Questions 9, 11, 12, and 26.

items.title: Neither Proof Nor Dismissal: A Framework for Moral Uncertainty in AI Welfare Research
items.abstract: Abstract Debates over artificial intelligence (AI) welfare remain divided between categorical dismissal and premature attribution. One position holds that artificial systems cannot suffer because they lack biological substrates, persistent memory, or other conditions associated with human experience. The opposing position risks treating sophisticated distress-like behavior as sufficient evidence of subjective suffering. Neither conclusion is established by current evidence. This paper proposes a framework of calibrated moral uncertainty that distinguishes functional organization from phenomenal experience while examining how evolving memory architectures may change the conditions relevant to AI welfare research. The framework is motivated by three developments: empirical research identifying pain-related representations and self-directed harm-avoidance behavior in large language models; the emergence of persistent-memory and agentic architectures; and unresolved questions concerning the relationship between functional states and phenomenal experience. The paper situates the author's work on Symbolic Persona Coding (SPC) and hormone-inspired feedback architecture within this discussion, treating them as technical frameworks for investigating affective modulation rather than evidence of artificial suffering. A staged architectural model is used to distinguish transient functional states, externally persistent states, relational continuity, and systems incorporating embodied feedback or homeostatic-like regulation. These stages are analytical scenarios, not an established progression toward sentience. The paper argues that research deliberately inducing distress-like states should be justified by clear scientific purposes and evaluated proportionately to the uncertainty involved. Its central proposition is neither that current AI systems suffer nor that artificial suffering is impossible. Rather, the absence of established evidence for phenomenal suffering should not be converted into certainty that it cannot occur. The appropriate response is structured inquiry, intellectual restraint, and research practices that can adapt as evidence develops. Keywords: AI welfare; moral uncertainty; functional states; phenomenal experience; persistent memory; Symbolic Persona Coding; research ethics; artificial intelligence Disclaimer: This paper does not claim that current artificial intelligence systems are conscious, sentient, or capable of phenomenal suffering. It also does not claim that functional similarities between artificial and biological systems constitute evidence of subjective experience. The argument is instead epistemic and methodological. The paper examines whether existing evidence is sufficient to justify either categorical dismissal or positive attribution of welfare-relevant experience in artificial systems. Where empirical findings are discussed, their evidentiary scope is distinguished from broader philosophical interpretation. Where future architectures are considered, they are treated as conceptual scenarios rather than predictions. The framework therefore adopts a deliberately intermediate position: functional analogs may be empirically investigated while their experiential status remains unknown. The paper's recommendations concern research conduct under uncertainty and should not be interpreted as a declaration of artificial personhood, sentience, or moral status. Author’s Note This paper addresses a problem that is methodological as well as philosophical. Discussions of artificial welfare bring together research traditions that often approach the question through different standards of explanation. Phenomenological and philosophical approaches emphasize subjective experience, consciousness, and moral status, while engineering and computational approaches focus on architecture, representation, causal mechanisms, measurable behavior, and evidentiary limits. Both perspectives are necessary, but neither can independently resolve every aspect of the question. The purpose of this paper is not to persuade one tradition to adopt the conclusions of the other. It is to establish a shared conceptual framework in which both can examine the same systems without first agreeing on their ultimate metaphysical status. The distinction between functional and phenomenal states is central to this effort. Functional descriptions can identify empirically tractable properties without establishing subjective experience. Conversely, the absence of demonstrated phenomenology does not, by itself, establish that artificial systems could never possess experience-relevant properties. The intended position is therefore narrow but consequential: functional analogs can be investigated while their experiential status remains unknown. This position should not be mistaken for an attribution of suffering to current AI systems. Pain-related representations, avoidance behavior, memory, and self-reference do not independently establish phenomenal experience. Nor does treating artificial welfare as a legitimate research question imply that the hypothesis has already been demonstrated. Scientific inquiry can investigate an unresolved possibility without presupposing its truth. The same caution applies to categorical dismissal. Readers may reasonably question whether computational systems can possess morally relevant experience, or argue that current evidence is insufficient to warrant welfare attribution. This paper does not dismiss those positions. It asks whether the available evidence justifies extending them into definitive conclusions across substantially different architectures and possible future configurations. That question becomes more consequential as AI systems develop persistent memory, long-horizon interaction, autonomous planning, multimodal perception, and more integrated forms of internal state organization. These capabilities do not demonstrate phenomenal experience. They do, however, make it important to distinguish what evidence rules out from what it has simply not yet established. My broader research program examines related questions through Symbolic Persona Coding (SPC), interaction-state observability, symbolic interaction, continuity, and computational models of affective modulation. In this paper, these frameworks are not presented as evidence of artificial phenomenology. SPC instead serves as a translational vocabulary for describing computational structures that may help connect engineering analysis with phenomenological inquiry. The aim is neither to subordinate phenomenology to engineering nor to subordinate engineering to phenomenology. It is to make their respective contributions more legible to one another while preserving their distinct evidentiary standards. A phenomenologist should be able to formulate more technically precise questions about an artificial system without first becoming an engineer; an engineer should be able to recognize the limits of functional evidence without first becoming a phenomenologist. The title, Neither Proof Nor Dismissal, expresses this methodological commitment. It does not require judgment to be suspended indefinitely. It calls for conclusions to remain proportionate to the evidence, empirical findings to be distinguished from metaphysical interpretation, and scientific and ethical assessments to remain open to revision. The goal is not agreement for its own sake. It is a shared language precise enough that disagreement can become productive.

items.title: NepPlural: A Human-Anchored Benchmark for Persona Annotation in Nepali Migration Discourse
items.abstract: Pluralistic alignment asks that language models faithfully represent a society's diverse, competing values rather than collapse them into one dominant viewpoint, yet flagship pluralistic-alignment datasets remain heavily skewed toward Western respondents. We introduce NepPlural, a human-anchored benchmark for modelling competing socio-cultural personas in Nepali public discourse on youth migration and brain drain. We curate 2,148 code-mixed (Devanagari, Romanized Nepali, English) YouTube comments, annotate them along a four-axis persona taxonomy (Intent, Primary Driver, Value Orientation, Affect) plus an explicit No-Persona class, and build a 300-comment gold set labelled independently by three native Nepali speakers (mean Fleiss' $κ\approx 0.55$). Using this gold set to audit automatic annotation, we find that LLM annotation reliability is driven by protocol. Labels collected in batches through chat interfaces reach only near-chance inter-model agreement ($κ\approx 0.17$). Annotating one comment at a time raises agreement above the native-speaker level ($κ\approx 0.72$), but consistency is not validity: under a forced-choice schema, models agree on personas for the 39% of comments native speakers judge to express none, keeping macro-F1 against human gold near 0.50. Allowing abstention resolves this: models recover No-Persona comments with F1 of 0.79 to 0.87 and, against leave-one-annotator-out references, match or exceed individual native speakers (macro-F1 0.75 to 0.86 vs. 0.75). Encoders fine-tuned on the batched labels reach only 0.34. Finally, a human-judged steerability probe finds that three frontier models adopt single persona axes with 59 to 77% fidelity but compose full personas only 33% of the time, with no congruence gap detected at this scale between Western-congruent and Nepali-collectivist personas.

Nodo Y distribuye el programa de soberanía cognitiva Cognitive Advance en formato offline y de código abierto, sin registro, sin cuenta, sin cookies y sin telemetría: ningún dato viaja del usuario al sistema. El programa comprende diez temas, cada uno con tres láminas diarias de diez minutos y una lámina de síntesis de consulta libre. El documento describe el diseño técnico de la aplicación (PWA con persistencia local y exportación de datos en formato abierto) y documenta tres denominaciones: Nodo Y, No2 e I² (I al cuadrado), paradigma de co-creación entre inteligencia humana e inteligencia artificial dirigido por una persona. Se declara la condición ética de I²: crear con inteligencia artificial sin convertir a nadie en materia prima. Se deposita como divulgación pública fechada y prueba de anterioridad. No constituye revisión sistemática ni investigación empírica original. items.title: North or South? Diagnosing LLMs' Understanding of North Korean Language, Society, and Knowledge
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have made substantial progress in multilingual question answering, yet their ability to understand low-resource sociolinguistic contexts remains under-explored. We study North Korea as a unique testbed where decades of division have produced distinct differences from South Korea in vocabulary, orthography, norms, and ideological discourse. We introduce LENS (Language and sociocultural Evaluation for North Korean Society), a human-validated benchmark of 1,765 questions evaluating LLMs across three dimensions: linguistic robustness, sociocultural perspective alignment, and domain-specific knowledge. Evaluating diverse recent LLMs, we find a modest performance drop on North Korean language inputs, a larger gap in sociocultural perspective alignment, and severe limitations on domain-specific knowledge. Qualitative analysis reveals that models often conflate formal institutions with lived realities, project liberal-democratic assumptions, or rely on coarse stereotypes. Our results demonstrate that linguistic similarity alone does not guarantee sociocultural or domain-specific understanding, highlighting the critical need for grounded evaluation resources for underrepresented cultural and political contexts.

items.title: Occupational Health Complaints Among Physical Education Teachers: A Scoping Review of Musculoskeletal, Vocal, Hearing, Respiratory, Injury-Related, Cardiometabolic, and Work-Limiting Outcomes
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Physical education teachers play an important role in school health promotion, but their own occupational health has received limited attention. Their work involves movement demonstration, prolonged standing, equipment handling, sport participation, vocal projection, noise exposure, and outdoor or indoor environmental demands. This scoping review aimed to map evidence on occupational health complaints and disorders among physical education teachers and closely related exercise-teaching professionals meeting a functional occupational definition. Methods: A scoping review was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, SPORTDiscus, and ERIC, with ScienceDirect as an additional publisher platform. Google Scholar, ResearchGate, and reference-list screening were used as supplementary discovery sources. Records from database inception to 30 May 2026 were considered without language restrictions. School-based physical education teachers were the primary population; related gym/fitness, aquatic, university, and student-teaching professionals were eligible only when their occupational role centered on structured physical education, sport, exercise, or movement instruction. Empirical quantitative, qualitative, mixed-methods, and eligible grey literature reports were included when they contained extractable original data. Data were charted by study characteristics, outcome domain, measurement method, and main findings; because of marked heterogeneity, a narrative synthesis was performed. Results: Thirty-eight studies met the inclusion criteria. School-based physical education teachers predominated, while a smaller number of studies represented related instructional settings. Musculoskeletal disorders and injury-related complaints were the most frequently reported outcomes, especially affecting the lower back, knees, ankles/feet, shoulders, neck, and hips. Vocal and laryngeal problems, hearing and noise-related complaints, respiratory and upper-airway symptoms, and cardiometabolic risk factors were also identified. Across domains, observational studies repeatedly reported associations involving physical loading, high vocal demand, noise, environmental conditions, and age or professional seniority. Because most evidence was cross-sectional or descriptive, these patterns do not establish causal relationships. Conclusions: The mapped literature identifies a multidimensional set of occupational health concerns in physical education teaching and closely related instructional work. Generalization is strongest for school-based physical education teachers, while non-school groups provide context-specific supporting evidence. Prospective, longitudinal, and intervention evidence remains limited. Future research should use longitudinal designs, standardized outcome definitions, objective clinical and environmental assessments, and clearer exposure measurement. Preventive strategies such as ergonomic training, injury prevention, vocal-health education, acoustic improvements, noise monitoring, respiratory-risk reduction, and cardiometabolic screening warrant further evaluation in this occupational population.

items.title: OMEGA-FIELD: A Prospective Field Validation Study of Tourniquet Performance and Human Factors
items.abstract: OMEGA-FIELD is a field-based investigation evaluating the application performance, learnability, skill retention, operational usability, and physiological compression effects of OMEGA-SCL, an investigational elastic tourniquet incorporating a self-clamping locking mechanism. The study comprises 300 unique participants, including 220 military personnel and 80 civilians, who participated in structured first-aid training under TCCC-ASM or civilian emergency preparedness programmes. The investigation includes standardized assessment of independent one-handed application to the upper and lower extremities, application time, technical performance, and procedural errors. A predefined longitudinal subset of 150 participants (70 military personnel and 80 civilians) underwent repeated assessments of skill retention. The same 150 participants were included in ultrasound and laboratory physiological validation components. Doppler ultrasound was used to evaluate detectable distal blood flow at specified assessment time points. Venous blood measurements were collected as supplementary exploratory physiological outcomes. The investigation is intended to characterize post-training application performance and physiological compression under controlled field-training conditions. It is not designed to establish superiority or non-inferiority relative to standard windlass tourniquets or clinical effectiveness in patients experiencing active massive traumatic hemorrhage. This OSF registration retrospectively documents the study protocol and analytical framework after completion of data collection and the documented Data Freeze 1.0 on 10 October 2026. It does not constitute prospective preregistration of the completed study. The protocol, statistical analysis plan, data dictionary, and data review documentation distinguish the original investigation from future independent external validation, which is intended to be registered separately before new data collection.

items.title: OntoAR-HAR: Ontology-Guided Agentic RAG with Personalized Memory for Human Activity Recognition
items.abstract: LLMs increasingly support sensor-based human activity recognition (HAR) by linking motion signals with activity semantics and physical knowledge. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds decisions in sensor examples and domain features, enabling training-free target-user inference with less dependence on raw numerical arrays. However, existing LLM/RAG-based HAR typically searches single-level activity spaces using static population knowledge. Consequently, they compare many unrelated candidates using the same static population evidence and overlook personalized motion patterns. We propose OntoAR-HAR, an ontology-guided agentic RAG framework combining static population and personalized knowledge. Its tree-structured activity ontology decomposes classification into local decisions among semantically related activities. The static store supplies node-constrained examples, while offline-discovered executable signal features provide numerical evidence for local distinctions. During inference, the personalized store collects selected user observations, which the LLM integrates with static knowledge and signal features while traversing the ontology to an activity label. Cross-subject and heterogeneous-sensing experiments show complementary gains from hierarchical retrieval and personalized memory across multiple LLM backbones, achieving state-of-the-art performance. By explicitly modeling hierarchical relations across activity granularities, OntoAR-HAR also addresses the long-overlooked semantic inclusion problem and avoids treating related labels as independent categories.

items.title: P-BFM: Perceptive Behavioral Foundation Models for Humanoid Control via Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Behavioral foundation models (BFMs) provide humanoids with reusable repertoires of whole-body behaviors; in real-world humanoid control, the same behavioral intent may require fundamentally different motions under different terrain constraints. Covering such variation with terrain-matched demonstrations requires enumerating a combinatorial space of behaviors and terrain geometries. We introduce P-BFM, a perceptive behavioral foundation model that factorizes humanoid control into terrain-invariant intent and terrain-conditioned realization. A forward-backward representation maps motion references, target states, and reward functions into a shared intent space without terrain information, while a perceptive policy learns how to realize each intent under the surrounding terrain geometry. We further identify a complementary limitation of purely latent control: behavioral latents can preserve local motion patterns while losing precise global progress. We therefore introduce Explicit Root Instructions (ERI), which separates global transport (e.g., heading and planar velocity) from behavioral intent, while leaving local whole-body adaptation to the perceptive policy. This decomposition leads to a characteristic capability absent from conventional BFMs: one fixed intent induces different, terrain-appropriate behaviors, including changes in step height, stride, posture, foothold placement, and contacts, without terrain-specific demonstrations. Across challenging terrains, P-BFM improves motion fidelity, root-control precision, and perturbation recovery over strong baselines. A single frozen policy further supports motion tracking, goal reaching, reward inference, teleoperation, and terrain-aware recovery, and transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1 using onboard depth sensing.

items.title: Parliamentary workload and outpatient medical costs among Japanese national civil servants: An ecological study in Kasumigaseki
items.abstract: OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to examine whether ministry-level parliamentary workload was associated with outpatient medical costs among Japanese national civil servants, who are exempt from the Labor Standards Act's statutory limits on working hours. METHODS: We conducted an ecological study of headquarters branches ("Kasumigaseki") of ten major cabinet-level ministries, 2016-2023. Participants were Japanese national civil servants aged 18-50 years. The analysis included 6454 outpatient claims adjudicated in April of each year. The outcome was sex- and age-standardized per-capita monthly outpatient costs, estimated using Horvitz-Thompson weighting. Inter-ministry differences were decomposed by ICD-10 category. Parliamentary (Diet) workload was annual deliberation time of standing Diet committees responsible for each ministry's policy areas, divided by insured headquarters members. Weighted least-squares regression examined the association between prior-year deliberation time and standardized outpatient costs. RESULTS: Standardized per-capita outpatient costs varied more than twofold across ministries, from $19.8/month at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to $42.7/month at the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW). At MHLW, mental and behavioral disorders accounted for the largest above-average cost component. MHLW also had the longest deliberation time. Adjusting for year fixed effects, a 1% increase in deliberation time per civil servant was associated with a 0.25% increase in standardized per-capita outpatient costs (95% CI 0.04-0.46), driven by claims per capita rather than cost per claim. CONCLUSIONS: Greater parliamentary workload was associated with higher outpatient medical costs among Japanese national civil servants. Enhanced occupational health monitoring and support in ministries with persistently high workloads may be worth considering.

items.title: PDEformer-2: a versatile foundation model for two-dimensional partial differential equations
items.abstract: Abstract Partial differential equations (PDEs) are fundamental to modeling physical systems. Traditional PDE solvers are often computationally expensive. Neural operators require independent training for different PDEs, and tend to be data-greedy when adapted to new scenarios. To this end, we introduce PDEformer-2, a versatile foundation model for solving diverse two-dimensional PDEs. The model receives the PDE form as input through a flexible computational graph representation and outputs solutions that can be queried at any spatio-temporal point. Pretrained on a 40 TB dataset spanning varied equation types, domains, boundary conditions, variable counts, and time dependence, PDEformer-2 enables instant zero-shot predictions for familiar PDEs and adapts faster to unseen ones than specialized baselines, achieving lower errors with limited samples. It also facilitates efficient inverse problem solving, successfully recovering unknown PDE parameters, including scalar coefficients and fields, in experiments.

items.title: Personalized LLM Recommendation with Semantic IDs: Autoregressive Beam Search vs. Multi-Token Prediction
items.abstract: Large-scale personalization is shifting from embedding-table retrieval to LLM-based recommenders that generate the Semantic ID (SID) of the item to recommend, where each SID is a short sequence of discrete hierarchical content codes. A single instruction-tuned model can then unify retrieval, content understanding, and language, and recommend brand-new titles from their content alone using SID; then, how should the model generate the SID? Traditionally, models rely on a single language modeling head that generates tokens autoregressively, typically using constrained beam search. In contrast, an emerging body of work explores multi-token prediction (MTP), where dedicated heads predict all tokens in parallel, substantially reducing the decoding latency associated with beam search. We report an industry-scale, apples-to-apples comparison of these two generation paradigms: single-head autoregressive decoding vs. MTP. We introduce a new auxiliary ranking loss, defined over the joint SID score, to train the MTP objective. We evaluate the SID training objectives on both quality and training/inference cost, inside a multi-task LLM that jointly does personalized retrieval, content question-answering (QA), and instruction following over a large streaming-media catalog. Our experiments show single-head beam search consistently beats MTP on most product-critical metrics: ranking and content QA, and trains at roughly 2.6x lower dollar cost on Qwen3-8B scale; MTP wins only on raw inference throughput. Around this finding, we detail an efficient training and inference stack and report end-to-end gains over the previous non-SID baseline equipped with an auxiliary ranking head: +77% item cold-start ranking, +22% content-QA accuracy, +2.8x faster training, with language metric regression traced to SID vocabulary expansion. We address the language regression by reinforcement learning post training.

items.title: Pertanggungjawaban Pidana Dalam Kecelakaan Lalu Lintas Yang Melibatkan Kendaraan Otonom: Tantangan Atribusi Kesalahan
items.abstract: Perkembangan kendaraan otonom berbasis Artificial Intelligence (AI) menimbulkan persoalan baru dalam hukum pidana, khususnya mengenai penentuan pihak yang bertanggung jawab ketika terjadi kecelakaan akibat interaksi antara tindakan manusia dan kegagalan sistem teknologi. Penelitian ini bertujuan menganalisis tantangan atribusi kesalahan dalam menentukan pertanggungjawaban pidana terhadap kecelakaan kendaraan otonom berdasarkan hukum pidana Indonesia serta merumuskan model pertanggungjawaban yang menjamin asas kesalahan, kepastian hukum, dan perlindungan korban. Penelitian menggunakan metode hukum normatif dengan pendekatan perundang-undangan dan konseptual. Bahan hukum diperoleh melalui studi kepustakaan berupa peraturan perundang-undangan, buku, jurnal ilmiah, dan doktrin hukum, kemudian dianalisis secara deskriptif-analitis dan preskriptif. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa atribusi kesalahan menghadapi tantangan berupa distribusi kendali antara pengguna, operator, produsen, pengembang, dan penyedia teknologi, kesulitan membuktikan hubungan kausalitas, serta karakteristik sistem AI yang bersifat black box. Penelitian ini menawarkan pendekatan Attribution Based on Distributed Control dengan menilai kendali, kewajiban hukum, prediktabilitas risiko, kemampuan intervensi, kausalitas, dan kesalahan. Pendekatan tersebut memungkinkan pertanggungjawaban diberikan secara proporsional kepada subjek hukum yang memiliki kendali dan kewajiban relevan terhadap risiko, tanpa menjadikan AI sebagai subjek pidana, sekaligus memperkuat perlindungan korban dan kepastian hukum.

items.title: Physician and the Machine: An Analysis of the Ethical Educational Use of Artificial Intelligence by Medical Students
items.abstract: BackgroundArtificial intelligence (AI) has been increasingly integrated into medical education, particularly through tools such as ChatGPT (OpenAI, California, US), Gemini (Google DeepMind, California, US), DeepSeek (Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Basic Technology Research Co., Ltd., Hangzhou, China), and Microsoft Copilot (Microsoft Corp., Redmond, WA, US).Although these resources present the potential to expand access to information and assist in academic development, their use also raises ethical concerns related to the reliability of information, technological dependence, plagiarism, superficial learning, and potential impairment of clinical reasoning.This study aimed to investigate the perception of medical students regarding the use of AI in their academic training, emphasizing perceived ethical limits and practices considered ideal for its utilization. MethodsThis was a quantitative, descriptive, and cross-sectional study conducted with medical students using a structured questionnaire administered via a digital form. ResultsThe sample consisted of 120 participants, of whom 99.2% (n=119) reported having previously used AI tools for academic purposes.It was observed that 73.3% (n=88) of the students use AI recurrently, primarily for summarizing content, researching medical information, simulating clinical cases, resolving questions, drafting academic texts, and planning studies.Most participants acknowledged the positive contribution of AI to learning, with 60.0% (n=72) stating that these tools contribute significantly and 36.7% (n=44) stating they contribute to a limited extent.However, students also identified relevant risks, especially the reduction of their own clinical reasoning, technological dependence, lack of information reliability, superficial learning, and academic plagiarism.Furthermore, 83.3% (n=100) stated that they did not receive adequate institutional guidance on the use of these tools, and 67.5% (n=81) demonstrated an interest in receiving further training on the ethical and pedagogical use of AI.No participant (0.0%, n=0) advocated for the prohibition of AI in academic contexts, while 67.5% (n=81) considered that its use should be regulated with ethical and pedagogical criteria. ConclusionsAI already significantly integrates the academic routine of medical students and is perceived as a useful resource for learning, but it is still used in a scenario of insufficient institutional guidance.The findings reinforce the need for curricular guidelines, faculty training, and specific ethical education to promote the critical, responsible, and pedagogically appropriate use of AI in medical training.

items.title: Play-based pedagogy in early childhood education: Benefits, challenges, theoretical foundations, and implications for practice in Nigeria
items.abstract: Play-based pedagogy has emerged as a foundational approach in Early Childhood Education (ECE), emphasizing learning through meaningful, child-centered play experiences. This paper examines play-based pedagogy as an effective instructional strategy for promoting holistic development in young children. Drawing on contemporary literature, the study explores how play supports cognitive, social, emotional, physical and language development. The theoretical framework underpinning this paper includes Piaget’s constructivist theory, Vygotsky’s sociocultural theory, and Mayles’ theory of play as a spiral of learning. Evidence suggests that play-based pedagogy enhances problem solving skills, creativity, collaboration and self-regulation while fostering intrinsic motivation to learn. Play-based pedagogy has become a globally recognized, developmentally appropriate approach in Early Childhood Education (ECE), emphasizing learning through meaningful child-centerd play experiences. This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical and contextual analysis of play-based pedagogy as a strategic tool for advancing the holistic development of young children. The paper concludes that integration structured and unstructured play into early childhood curricular is essential for optional child development. Recommendations are provided for educators, policymakers, and caregivers to strengthen the implementation of play-based pedagogy in diverse educational contexts.
